title: K Divisible Elements Subarrays
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` and integers `k` and `p`. Consider every non-empty contiguous slice (subarray) of `nums` that contains **no more than `k`** elements divisible by `p`. Return how many **different** such subarrays there are.

Two subarrays are the same only when they have equal length and equal values at every position; where they sit inside `nums` does not matter. So a sequence of values that shows up several times is counted once.
signature: int countDistinct(int[] nums, int k, int p)
notes:
## Intuition

There are only about n²/2 subarrays, and with n at most 200 that is roughly 20,000, so listing all of them is affordable. Two things remain: rejecting subarrays with too many multiples of `p`, and counting each sequence of values only once.

Fix a starting index and grow the subarray one element to the right at a time. The number of multiples of `p` can only rise as it grows, so once it passes `k` every longer subarray from that start fails too and the inner loop can stop. To remove repeats, turn each subarray into a text key and put it in a set; equal sequences give equal keys. The key is extended by one value per step rather than rebuilt, and a comma after every value keeps `[1, 23]` and `[12, 3]` apart.

## Approach

1. Create an empty set `seen`.
2. For each `start`, reset `divisible` to 0 and `key` to an empty string.
3. Move `end` from `start` to the right. If `nums[end]` is a multiple of `p`, increase `divisible`.
4. If `divisible` exceeds `k`, stop extending this start.
5. Otherwise append `nums[end]` and a comma to `key` and add `key` to `seen`.
6. Return the size of `seen`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 3, 3, 2, 2]`, `k = 2`, `p = 2`.

- `start = 0`: keys `"2,"`, `"2,3,"`, `"2,3,3,"`, `"2,3,3,2,"` are added; the last `2` makes `divisible = 3`, so the loop breaks. Set size 4.
- `start = 1`: `"3,"`, `"3,3,"`, `"3,3,2,"`, `"3,3,2,2,"` are new. Size 8.
- `start = 2`: `"3,"` is already there; `"3,2,"` and `"3,2,2,"` are new. Size 10.
- `start = 3`: `"2,"` exists; `"2,2,"` is new. Size 11.
- `start = 4`: `"2,"` exists. The answer is `11`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³) in the worst case: about n² keys are created and hashing a key costs up to its length. With n ≤ 200 this is fast. A trie over the values brings it to O(n²).
- Space: O(n³) characters for the stored keys in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Count different value sequences, not different positions: `[2]` at index 0 and at index 3 is one subarray.
- Without a separator, keys like `"123"` could come from `[1, 23]` or `[12, 3]`.
- Check `divisible > k` before adding the key, so the subarray that breaks the limit is never stored.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | set of keys of the valid subarrays found so far |
| `start`, `end` | first and last index of the current subarray |
| `divisible` | how many elements of the current subarray are multiples of `p` |
| `key` | the current subarray written as comma-separated text |

narration.2: The set keeps one key per different sequence of values, so repeats collapse automatically.
narration.4: Try every index as the first element of a subarray.
narration.5: A new start begins with no multiples of p counted.
narration.6: The key for the empty prefix is an empty string; it grows with each element.
narration.7: Extend the subarray one element to the right at a time.
narration.8: Is the new element a multiple of p?
narration.9: Yes: one more divisible element in this subarray.
narration.11: Too many multiples of p; longer subarrays from this start would only have more.
narration.14: Append the value and a separator so different sequences never share a key.
narration.15: Record this valid subarray; an identical sequence seen earlier adds nothing.
narration.18: The set size is the number of different valid subarrays.
